title: Reaction rate
summary: How is rate measured, what does it depend on and what does a catalyst do?
cards.0.p: Reaction rate is the change in concentration per unit time. For A → B we write r = −Δ[A]/Δt = Δ[B]/Δt, and the unit is M/s. The slope of the curve at a single point is called the instantaneous rate.
cards.0.key: Reactants are used up, so Δ[reactant] is negative. A minus sign is put in front, so the rate is always positive. The change between two moments is called the average rate.
cards.1.p: Instead of concentration, an easy-to-measure property is tracked. This property must change as the reaction goes on. Volume of gas released, pressure, color, conductivity or mass in an open container can be tracked.
cards.1.svg#2: volume of H₂ released grows over time
cards.1.svg#5: constant V, T: 3 mol gas → 2 mol, pressure drops
cards.1.svg#8: red-brown Br₂ is used up, color fades
cards.1.svg#14: in an open container CO₂ escapes, mass drops
cards.1.key: If the moles of gas don't change (as in H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr), the rate can't be tracked by pressure.
cards.1.once.soru: A Mg ribbon dissolves in HCl solution, releasing H₂ gas. What is the easiest way to track the rate?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.yazi: By the volume of gas released
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: As H₂ is released, its volume can be measured. The increase in volume per unit time shows the rate.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.yazi: By the color of the solution
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: Both HCl and MgCl₂ solutions are colorless. So the color doesn't change.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.yazi: By the volume of the solution
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: The volume of the solution doesn't change noticeably.
cards.2.p: The reaction aA → bB has a single rate, found from r = −(1/a)·Δ[A]/Δt = (1/b)·Δ[B]/Δt. The rates at which substances are used up and formed are proportional to their coefficients.
cards.2.key: The ratio of the rates equals the ratio of the coefficients. For N₂, H₂ and NH₃, for example, this ratio is 1 : 3 : 2.
cards.3.p: For a reaction, particles must collide, but only a few collisions give products. An effective collision needs enough kinetic energy and the right orientation.
cards.3.key: Enough energy and the right orientation together make an effective collision. The rate depends on the number of effective collisions per unit time.
cards.4.p: The minimum energy needed for an effective collision is called the activation energy (Ea). At the top of the hill, an unstable, short-lived activated complex forms. If Ea is large, the reaction is usually slow.
cards.4.svg#8: old bonds weaken, new ones form
cards.4.key: In the activated complex, old bonds weaken and new ones begin to form.
cards.4.once.soru: Paper releases heat when it burns, but it doesn't catch fire by itself on a desk. Why?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: Exothermic reactions also have an activation energy. A match supplies this energy.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: Burning releases heat, so it is exothermic.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: There is enough oxygen in the air.
cards.5.p: The forward and reverse reactions pass over the same hill. The difference gives the heat of reaction: ΔH = Ea,forward − Ea,reverse. In an exothermic reaction, Ea,forward is smaller.
cards.5.key: In an endothermic reaction Ea,forward > Ea,reverse, because ΔH > 0.
cards.5.once.soru: In an exothermic reaction, from which direction is it harder to climb the hill?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: The products have lower energy. Climbing the hill from the products takes more energy.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: The reactants are at high energy and closer to the top.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: The reactants and products have different energies, so the heights differ.
cards.6.p: The rate law has the form rate = k[A]x[B]y. x and y are found by experiment, and in elementary reactions they equal the coefficients. Solids and pure liquids are not written in the rate law.
cards.6.key: The overall order is x + y. k doesn't change with concentration, but it does change with temperature and catalysts.
cards.6.once.soru: In the one-step reaction 2A → B, if [A] doubles, by what factor does the rate change?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: In an elementary reaction the order equals the coefficient, so rate = k[A]². The rate goes up 2² = 4 times.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: The rate is proportional to the square of [A], not linear.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: When concentration rises, the number of collisions rises.
cards.7.p: Compare two experiments in which only one substance's concentration changes. If doubling the concentration doubles the rate, the order is 1. If the rate goes up 4 times, the order is 2.
cards.7.svg#19: rate = k[X][Y]²   (3rd order; not equal to coefficients)
cards.7.etk.soru: For this reaction rate = k[X][Y]<sup>2</sup>, k = 2 L²/(mol²·s). Double [X] or [Y]: by what factor does the rate go up?
cards.7.key: If the concentration goes up n times, the rate goes up nˣ times. If doubling the concentration makes the rate 4 times larger, x = 2.
cards.8.p: The unit of rate is always M/s. The unit of k depends on the overall order. It is M/s for zero order, 1/s for first order and 1/(M·s) for second order.
cards.8.key: If the unit of k is M/s, the reaction is zero order. Then the rate doesn't depend on concentration.
cards.8.once.soru: For rate = k[A], rate is in M/s and [A] in M. What is the unit of k?
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: M/s is the unit of rate. The unit of k comes from dividing it by [A].
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: k relates to rate, so its unit must include time.
cards.9.p: Most reactions happen in several steps, and these steps are called the mechanism. The overall rate is set by the slowest step, the one with the largest Ea. The rate law is written from the reactants of this step.
cards.9.key: An intermediate that forms in one step and is used up in the next is not written in the rate law.
cards.9.once.soru: On a production line, three machines work in sequence: 100, 10 and 50 items per hour. Which one sets the speed of the line?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: Items pile up at the slowest machine. The line can't run faster than this machine.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: The fast machine waits for the slow one after it.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: In sequential work, the slowest step sets the overall speed.
cards.10.p: Reactions between oppositely charged ions are very fast. The more bonds that must break, the slower the reaction. When concentration rises, the number of collisions rises and so does the rate.
cards.10.key: For gases, reducing the volume raises the concentration. The concentration of a substance with zero order doesn't change the rate.
cards.10.once.soru: Charcoal burns slowly in air but quickly with a bright flame in pure oxygen. Why?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: There is more O₂ per unit volume. So the number of collisions and the rate go up.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: Ea is changed by a catalyst, not by concentration.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.yazi: The charcoal gives off more heat
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: It is the same reaction, and the heat released is the same. Only the rate is different.
cards.11.p: When temperature rises, particles speed up. The main effect, though, is that a larger fraction of particles exceeds E<sub>a</sub>. E<sub>a</sub> doesn't change, but k gets larger. That's why the rate goes up in both exothermic and endothermic reactions.
cards.11.svg#7: The total area under the curves (number of particles) is the same.
cards.11.key: Roughly, every 10 °C rise about doubles the rate of many reactions.
cards.12.p: Heterogeneous reactions, such as solid–solution ones, happen only at the contact surface. Grinding a solid into powder increases the surface, so collisions and the rate go up.
cards.12.svg#4: Same mass, twice the surface: powder is faster
cards.12.key: Flour dust in the air can explode from a spark. Surface area plays no role in gas–gas reactions.
cards.13.p: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by opening a new path with a lower Ea, and it comes out of the reaction unchanged. The forward and reverse rates both go up, but ΔH doesn't change.
cards.13.svg#6: Forward and reverse Eₐ drop by the same amount.
cards.13.key: The amount of product doesn't change either. The catalysts in living things are enzymes.
cards.14.p: A catalyst in the same phase as the reactants is homogeneous, and one in a different phase is heterogeneous. Substances that slow a reaction down are called inhibitors. Food preservatives delay spoilage this way.
cards.14.key: I⁻ dissolved in water speeds up H₂O₂ as a homogeneous catalyst, and solid MnO₂ as a heterogeneous one. The solid Pt and Pd in a catalytic converter are also heterogeneous catalysts.
cards.14.once.soru: What do preservatives added to food do to spoilage reactions?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: Preservatives are inhibitors and delay spoilage.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: A substance that speeds up a reaction is a catalyst.
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.neden: If they had no effect, they wouldn't be added to food.
cards.15.p:
• Rate is the change in concentration per unit time, and the rates of substances are proportional to the coefficients.
• An effective collision needs enough energy and the right orientation.
• ΔH = Ea,forward − Ea,reverse. A catalyst lowers Ea and doesn't change ΔH.
• The rate law is rate = k[A]x[B]y, and the orders are found by experiment.
cards.15.svg#16: ΔH: unchanged in all three (including catalyst)
quiz.0.q: The rate law of X + 2Y → Z is rate = k[X]<sup>2</sup>[Y]. At the same temperature, if [X] is tripled and [Y] is halved, by what factor does the rate change?
quiz.0.e: The rate changes by 3² × ½ = 4.5 times. The orders come from the rate law, not from the coefficients of the equation.
quiz.1.q: For a reaction between a solid and a solution, sort each change by its effect on the rate.
quiz.1.e: As temperature rises, more particles exceed E<sub>a</sub>. A catalyst opens a path with lower E<sub>a</sub>. A powdered solid has a larger contact surface. An inhibitor, low temperature and small contact surface slow the reaction.
quiz.2.q: For a reaction, E<sub>a,forward</sub> = 120 kJ and E<sub>a,reverse</sub> = 45 kJ. What is ΔH for the reaction in kJ?
quiz.2.e: ΔH = E<sub>a,forward</sub> − E<sub>a,reverse</sub> = 120 − 45 = +75 kJ. The result is positive, so the reaction is endothermic. The products are 75 kJ higher than the reactants.
quiz.3.q: The reaction 2NO + Br<sub>2</sub> → 2NOBr has two steps: 1) NO + Br<sub>2</sub> → NOBr<sub>2</sub> (slow), 2) NOBr<sub>2</sub> + NO → 2NOBr (fast). Which is the rate law?
quiz.3.e: The slow step sets the rate. The reactants of this step are one NO and one Br<sub>2</sub>, so rate = k[NO][Br<sub>2</sub>]. The second NO enters in the fast step and doesn't affect the rate.
quiz.3.y.0: You took the exponents from the coefficients of the net equation. The rate law is written from the slow step, which has only one NO.
quiz.3.y.2: NOBr<sub>2</sub> is an intermediate. Intermediates are not written in the rate law.
quiz.3.y.3: Br<sub>2</sub> takes part in the slow step and can't be left out of the rate law.
A:ozet: Watch the concentration curve and collide molecules. Try temperature and a catalyst, then find the rate law from experiments.
A:adimlar.0.metin: The reaction A → B is starting. Press play and watch the slope of the curve.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: What happens to the rate as the reaction goes on?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The rate depends on the concentration of the reactants. As A is used up, there are fewer particles to collide, so the rate doesn't increase.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: As A runs out, the number of collisions drops and the slope flattens. The rate is highest at the start.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: A constant rate would mean the curve is a straight line. But the curve keeps flattening.
A:adimlar.1.metin: Rates are proportional to the coefficients. In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, H₂ is used up at 0.6 M/s. Set the rate at which NH₃ forms.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: Rates are proportional to the coefficients. While 3 mol of H₂ is used up, 2 mol of NH₃ forms.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: 0.6 × 2/3 = 0.4 M/s. Rates are proportional to the coefficients: 0.2 M/s for N₂, 0.6 for H₂ and 0.4 for NH₃. Dividing each by its coefficient gives the same reaction rate, 0.2 M/s.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Ea is the minimum energy for a collision to give products. In the reaction AB + C → A + BC, Ea = 60 kJ. Set the energy and the orientation, then press play.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: The energy reached Ea and C hit the B end. This is an effective collision. Very few collisions are effective, so not every collision gives products.
A:adimlar.3.metin: The curve shows how the particles are spread over energies. The shaded area shows the particles above Ea. Raise the temperature and see what changes.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: Why does the rate rise when temperature rises?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The Ea line didn't move. Temperature doesn't shift the threshold, it increases the number of particles past it.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The number of particles in the container is the same. So the total area under the curve doesn't change.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The curve spreads to the right and the shaded area grows. So the number of effective collisions per unit time increases.
A:adimlar.4.metin: The same mass of marble (CaCO₃) is dropped into HCl. In one flask the marble is in lumps, in the other it is powdered. The CO₂ released will inflate balloons.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: With lumps, the acid touches only the outer surface. A small surface means few collisions.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: More CaCO₃ particles collide with the acid per unit time, so CO₂ comes out fast. The mass is the same, so in the end both balloons inflate equally.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: In the end the total CO₂ released is the same, but the surface decides how fast it comes out.
A:adimlar.5.metin: A and B particles are colliding in the container. An orange flash shows an effective collision that gives products. The curve on the right is the energy spread of the particles, and the shaded part shows those above Ea. Change the concentration, the temperature and the catalyst.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.bulgular.0.yazi: At 300 K, double the concentration of A and B. By what factor did the rate change?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.bulgular.0.tamam: The rate went up 4 times. Both A and B doubled, so A–B collisions went up 2 × 2 = 4 times. For this reaction, rate = k[A][B].
A:adimlar.5.gorev.bulgular.1.yazi: At concentration 1, raise the temperature from 300 K to just 310 K.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.bulgular.1.tamam: A 10 K rise made the rate about 1.9 times larger. The particles sped up a little, but the main reason is that the part of the curve above Ea grew.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.bulgular.2.yazi: At 300 K and concentration 1, add a catalyst.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.bulgular.2.tamam: The catalyst lowered Ea from 50 kJ to 40 kJ and the threshold moved left. Without any change in temperature, the rate went up about 55 times. A catalyst comes out of the reaction unchanged.
A:adimlar.6.metin: [X] is kept constant. Increase [Y] and watch by what factor the rate changes.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: What is the order of the reaction in Y?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: If it were first order, doubling [Y] would double the rate. Here the rate goes up 4 times.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: If it were third order, doubling [Y] would make the rate 8 times larger.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: When [Y] doubled, the rate went up 4 times, and when it tripled, 9 times. The rate is proportional to [Y]², so y = 2.
A:kapanis.0: Reaction rate is the change in concentration per unit time (rate = −Δ[reactant]/Δt). The rates of substances are proportional to their coefficients.
A:kapanis.1: For a reaction to happen, a collision must be effective. The energy must exceed Ea and the orientation must be right.
A:kapanis.2: Temperature increases the fraction of particles above Ea. A larger contact surface speeds up heterogeneous reactions.
A:kapanis.3: A catalyst lowers Ea equally in both directions and doesn't change ΔH.
A:kapanis.4: The rate law is rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ. If doubling a concentration makes the rate 4 times larger, the order in that substance is 2.
